comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
I use it as a top-level orchestrator for my project. Two workflow examples:

When I'm implementing a substantial feature of the game (e.g., moving and shooting in an FPS), I start by talking to Fable a lot about what the feature kit should be, how it should feel in normal play, how to resolve the edge cases, stuff like that. One session that runs somewhat long but doesn't hit its sizable compaction window by any stretch. That session ends with it churning out a series of session plans for Opus, ideally scoped so that the work can get done before that session compacts. Then I swap to Opus sessions for each session plan, and that Opus session orchestrates for the actual coding agents. I do it this way because Fable can handle reading the entire project documentation and what we already did while providing coherent and insightful feedback, and can scope things into Opus-sized chunks.

When I'm creating 3D assets, I start with a Fable session to hammer out what exactly the asset is (or set of assets if they're simpler props that belong to one scene for instance). During that session, I draw whatever it is I'm making myself because I'm just barely able to clear that bar lol... but I regularly do shit that talented artists wouldn't, like having noticeable asymmetries in limbs or mangled hands/feet/other parts I'm just awful at drawing. I have Fable help me digitize the drawing into something easy to edit and then "clean up" the obvious mistakes, and we end up with a model sheet to feed to a mesh generator. Then we get several copies of the mesh, decide how it should be segmented, pick out the best version of each segment that was generated, and have GPT assemble it in Blender as our baseline with some basic showcasing (a jog animation to see it in motion plus stress pose stills to see where the mesh breaks). Finally, Fable and I cook up the "roadmap" for fixing the asset, scoped like the coding stuff I described above (Opus size iteration sessions). Fable is the best for this because it needs to keep several token-heavy images in context as well as a lot of art direction stuff from my art bible. These sessions can be long and chew up a lot of usage for one complex asset, but for my scope and timeline that's acceptable.

All that said, for sure I would not use Fable for more than just high level orchestration tasks like those, or perhaps things like a full codebase audit. Opus 5.5 is clearly more price-efficient while still delivering "good enough" quality output (really quite high quality output). You need to be getting mileage out of Fable's ability to handle obscenely fuckhuge context windows without getting lost.

As a model Fable 5.2 feels great to work with, it's just not available enough to waste on bullshit that Opus can do just as well.
